charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb Company: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Bristol-Myers Squibb Company: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb Company: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb Company: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

portfolioMix.title: Growth Portfolio vs Legacy Portfolio
portfolioMix.content:
BMY splits revenue into a Growth Portfolio (Opdivo, Breyanzi, Reblozyl, Camzyos, Opdualag, Cobenfy, Krazati, Augtyro, Sotyktu and other recent launches) and a Legacy Portfolio dominated by Eliquis and Revlimid, which are losing exclusivity.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb: the entire investment case is whether the Growth Portfolio's dollar additions outrun the Legacy Portfolio's dollar losses before Eliquis itself rolls over -- Legacy revenue fell from $25.7bn (FY2024) to $21.8bn (FY2025) while Growth rose from $22.6bn to $26.4bn, so the crossover has already happened at the portfolio level, but Eliquis (still ~$14.4bn, growing) is the next shoe to drop via IRA Medicare price negotiation and 2028 generic exposure.

What to watch:

  • Whether Growth Portfolio's YoY dollar gain still exceeds Legacy's YoY dollar loss each quarter
  • Eliquis specifically rolling over, since it is still growing and is by far the largest single product
  • The two filing layouts (this chart vs. older RevenueInlineProducts/RevenueNewProductPortfolio) are not directly comparable -- segment definitions changed

legacyDecline.title: Eliquis and Revlimid
legacyDecline.content:
Revlimid (multiple myeloma) lost US exclusivity in 2022 under a licensed-entry settlement and has collapsed from generic competition. Eliquis (anticoagulant, co-marketed with Pfizer) is BMY's largest product and faces both a 2028 patent cliff and IRA Medicare price negotiation (negotiated price effective 2026).

For Bristol-Myers Squibb: Revlimid fell from $12.8bn (FY2021) to $3.0bn (FY2025) -- a near-complete loss of ~$10bn of revenue in four years -- and is the template bear-case for what happens to Eliquis once it loses exclusivity. Eliquis is still growing ($14.4bn FY2025, up from $10.8bn FY2021) only because volume gains have outpaced the IRA price cut so far.

What to watch:

  • Any deceleration or reversal in Eliquis growth as the IRA negotiated price phases in
  • Revlimid's remaining base (~$3bn) as a floor for how fast an unprotected large-molecule-adjacent drug can fall

growthDrivers.title: Key growth-driver products
growthDrivers.content:
The named products BMY and analysts point to as replacing Legacy Portfolio revenue: Opdivo (immuno-oncology, BMY's largest growth product and itself facing a subcutaneous-reformulation patent strategy), Breyanzi and Reblozyl (cell therapy/hematology from the Celgene deal), Camzyos (cardiomyopathy), Opdualag (melanoma combination), Cobenfy (schizophrenia, launched 2024 via the Karuna acquisition) and Krazati (KRAS-mutant lung cancer, from Mirati).

For Bristol-Myers Squibb: Opdivo alone ($10.0bn FY2025) is larger than the other six combined, so its own patent exposure (core patents expire ~2028) matters as much as any newer launch; Cobenfy and Krazati are the true call-option growth names, each still under $250m FY2025 but scaling from a zero base.

What to watch:

  • Opdivo's growth rate specifically, since it is both a Growth Portfolio product and the next patent-cliff risk
  • Cobenfy and Krazati's ramp versus launch-year comparables for peer schizophrenia/KRAS drugs
  • Whether combined growth-driver additions keep clearing Legacy Portfolio's dollar decline

usIntl.title: US vs International revenue
usIntl.content:
Geographic split of total revenue between the US (where list prices are highest but IRA negotiation now applies) and International markets.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb: the US is the larger and more profitable market and the one directly exposed to IRA Medicare price negotiation; international growth is the diversification argument against US policy risk.

What to watch:

  • US revenue growth decelerating as IRA-negotiated prices phase in on more drugs
  • International share of revenue rising as a policy-risk offset

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb Company: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb Company: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb Company: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb Company: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Bristol-Myers Squibb Company: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
